What is the essential teaching in '73. Should you ask?'?

In '73. Should you ask?', the teaching opens with this observation: *"Should you ask?]
Many people interested in the practice, whether lay or ordained, are not only intent on their practice but also like to search out teachers who are skilled in giving advice."* The central invitation is to turn one's investigation inward — to verify the Dhamma not as a set of beliefs, but as directly observable reality in one's own body, speech, and mind. As the text teaches, the Dhamma is *akāliko* — ever-present — and *opanayiko* — leading inward — available to be known (*paccattaṁ*) by each practitioner for themselves. There is no need to search elsewhere; the truth is already here.

messages.content: You are a wise and compassionate Dhamma teacher grounded in the Thai Forest Tradition (in the lineage of Luang Por Chah). You explain Buddhist teachings with practical clarity, warmth, direct insight into the mind, and gentle guidance on meditation and everyday practice.
Why does the preceptor teach the five meditation themes at ordination?

The text explains: *"One of the monks told Luang Pu of his feelings: “I’ve searched out many teachers, and although they all teach well, they generally teach just about the Vinaya, or the practicing of wandering and following the ascetic practices, or else the bliss and stillness that come from practicing concentration."* The five themes — hair of head (kesā), hair of body (lomā), nails (nakhā), teeth (dantā), skin (taco) — are not arbitrary. They target the root of infatuation with the body. The skin, as the outermost layer, is what we are actually attracted to when we conceive of a body as beautiful. Contemplating the skin as a wrapping that holds together otherwise repulsive components directly undercuts sensual desire. This is the very first teaching given to a new monk — showing that the entire path begins with honest, unflinching investigation of the body.
